description: Who cares about Batman. Robin is the real deal. Be the SideKick!
summary: FireCal merges MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into one consistent record and shows it as a burning-activity calendar for any place on Earth, from November 2000 to yesterday. MODIS sees 1 km pixels and VIIRS sees 375 m pixels, so VIIRS reports roughly five to ten times as many hotspots over the same fires; counted raw, every region appears to catch fire in 2012. FireCal removes that step. For the area you draw or the country you pick, it learns a conversion factor for each satellite and each calendar month from the years the sensors flew together, and expresses everything in one unit: S-NPP VIIRS-equivalent hotspots. The result answers three questions: which months burn most, which years burned most, and how the latest month compares with the historical median. Every harmonisation is tested live by holding out each overlap year and asking MODIS alone to predict what VIIRS saw (monthly R² of 0.95 to 0.99 across five countries with very different fire regimes). Calendars and weighted hotspots download as CSV. Fire is one of the main ways stored carbon is lost, so a comparable fire history matters to land managers, researchers and carbon projects.
details:
What it does?

FireCal is a web tool, live at https://firecal.plotcarbon.com. Draw a rectangle or polygon on the map, pick a country, or type a bounding box, then press Build calendar. FireCal fetches the NASA FIRMS detections for that area and returns one harmonised series from November 2000 to yesterday as a month-by-year calendar. Around it are headline tiles (latest month against the median, the months that hold 80% of activity, the most active year, the long-term trend), a seasonal profile, annual totals, a day-by-day calendar, a hotspot density map, and CSV downloads of the calendar and of every hotspot with its harmonisation weight.

How the harmonisation works?

The common unit is the S-NPP VIIRS-equivalent hotspot: the number of detections the 375 m VIIRS instrument on Suomi NPP reports, or would have reported before it launched. Low-confidence detections, volcanoes and offshore sources are dropped. For each area, every other satellite gets a gain per calendar month, learned from the months it flew alongside S-NPP (S-NPP detections divided by that satellite's detections). The ratio is not a constant: small, cool agricultural burns that a 1 km MODIS pixel misses dominate some seasons and large wildfires dominate others, so gains are fitted per area and per month, and sparse months lean on the area's overall gain. MODIS is calibrated on 2012 to 2020 only, because Terra and Aqua have drifted to different overpass times since. Each day uses the best instrument tier available and pools it, so a satellite joining or dropping out does not shift the level of the series. Every hotspot carries a weight, which is why the map, the CSV and the calendar always add up to the same totals.

Reports Verified?

Each year of the 2012 to 2020 overlap is held out in turn, the gains are refitted without it, and MODIS alone is asked to predict what VIIRS saw that year. On Portugal, Greece, Ghana, Cambodia and Bolivia, where raw VIIRS counts are 5.7 to 10.3 times the MODIS counts, the harmonised series reaches a monthly R² of 0.95 to 0.99, an annual error of 3.5% to 8.4% and a bias within 1.5%. The same test runs live for whatever area the user selects and is shown in the app, so a region where the method struggles says so. Design choices were made by experiment: scaling raw detections beat counting unique grid cells, and calendar-month gains roughly halved the monthly error of a single gain.

Benefits and intended impact?

Anyone can read 25 years of fire history for a place without the artificial jump in 2012: which months burn most, which years burned most, and whether this month is unusual. That serves land managers, researchers and journalists, and carbon project developers, for whom fire is one of the main ways stored carbon is lost. FireCal is a Plot Carbon initiative and is open source under the Apache License 2.0.

Tools and languages used?

Python backend (FastAPI, NumPy, pandas) with an on-disk columnar store indexed by 0.25 degree tiles; a single-page front end in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet, Leaflet.draw and hand-written SVG charts; Docker and Caddy for deployment. Colour ramps run monotonically in lightness so they hold up under colour-vision deficiency, and every chart has hover and keyboard read-outs. The source code was written with the assistance of Claude.

The tool has limits -

Hotspots are detections, not fires or burned area. Dates are UTC. Satellite outages of a few days are not gap-filled. November 2000 to mid-2002 rests on Terra alone and is the least certain part of the record.
